extracted.intended_audience: IPR practitioners (petitioners and patent owners), PTAB judges and counsel in inter partes review proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Applying the PTAB's Fintiv discretionary-denial factors to decide whether to institute an IPR when parallel district-court litigation exists; argues why the Director should not deny institution here. Focuses on stays, trial scheduling, stage of litigation, overlap of issues, party status, and petition strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 1: The Parallel Litigation is Stayed
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the parallel district-court litigation has been stayed pending resolution of the IPR (i.e., a district court stay of the litigation pending PTAB resolution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A district court stay 'allays concerns about inefficiency and duplication of efforts' and thus strongly favors institution. The correct inquiry for Factor 1 is whether a stay has been granted — not speculation about what might happen if the stay is lifted. Example: court orders staying litigation pending resolution of the IPR weigh heavily in favor of institution. Anti-pattern: treating the factor as neutral because the stay might be lifted later. Citations: Apple Inc. v. Fintiv, Inc.; ResMed Corp. v. Cleveland Medical Devices, Inc.; Court Order (Ex. 1015).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 2: No Trial Date has been Scheduled
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a trial date in the parallel litigation has been set and the proximity of any scheduled trial to the Board’s projected Final Written Decision (FWD) deadline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no Rule 16(b) scheduling order has been entered, discovery has not begun, and no trial date has been set, Factor 2 favors institution. Trial statistics (median time-to-trial) may be consulted but are not controlling when the litigation is stayed and no scheduling order exists. The Board examines whether a trial would realistically occur before the FWD — mere statistical projections do not override a court-ordered stay. Also consider the district court's assessment of undue prejudice. Citations: ResMed Corp.; Stingray Group; Fintiv guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 3: The Parallel Litigation is in the Early Stages
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the parallel proceeding is still at an early stage (e.g., no exchange of contentions, no discovery, no Markman, no Rule 16(b) scheduling order, no answer due to pending motion to dismiss).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When litigation is in the early stages and party investments are nominal, Factor 3 favors institution. The Board considers petitioner diligence in filing the IPR, but the early-stage nature of the case can outweigh timing concerns about when the petition was filed. Filing routine motions (e.g., motion to dismiss) does not render the case advanced for purposes of Factor 3. Precedent: Stingray Group; Snap, Inc. anti-patterns: treating routine early litigation activity as evidence of advanced stage or undue prejudice when the court ordered a stay prior to scheduling/discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 4: Overlap Between IPR and Parallel Litigation Issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether there are overlapping issues between the IPR and the parallel district-court litigation and whether the IPR would simplify or dispose of issues in the court case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the IPR has the potential to simplify or dispose of claims (e.g., could dispose of claims as to two patents or eliminate counts in the complaint) and parties have not exchanged contentions, concerns of inefficiency and conflicting decisions are reduced — Factor 4 favors institution. The existence of a stay prior to scheduling/discovery/Markman further diminishes overlap concerns. Additional consideration: estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315 mitigates concerns because petitioner would be estopped from raising grounds raised or that reasonably could have been raised after a Final Written Decision. Arguments about lack of stipulations (Sotera/Sand) do not create overlap when the case is stayed early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 5: Petitioner Is Defendant in Parallel Litigation (Status of Parties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the petitioner is the defendant in the parallel litigation — a circumstance that traditionally favors discretionary denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although Factor 5 traditionally weighs in favor of denial when the petitioner is the defendant, this factor alone is insufficient to overcome Factors 1–4 where those factors strongly favor institution. The Board balances this factor against others; it does not automatically require denial. Example: ResMed Corp. where Factor 5 did not control the outcome when other factors favored institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 6: Strength/Weakness of the Petition
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the petition presents a strong prima facie case of unpatentability (adequate claim-element-by-element mapping to prior art, adequate articulation of grounds, and a Graham-style analysis), or conversely whether the petition is 'weak'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor 6 considers whether the petition is sufficiently detailed and persuasive: it must identify grounds for unpatentability, explain which references are relied on and how they map to each claim limitation, and provide supporting evidence (e.g., expert testimony). Mere attorney argument that a petition is 'weak' is insufficient absent demonstration of specific mapping or analytical deficiencies. If references were not considered during prosecution and the petition identifies that, this supports institution because it can show examiner error. Patent Owner attacks that fail to point to inadequate mappings or lack of grounds do not overcome the petition. The Board looks for an element-by-element explanation and evidence to support a prima facie case under Graham.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undue Prejudice to Patent Owner
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether the patent owner will suffer undue prejudice from instituting the IPR (examples include loss of evidence, unreasonable delay, or competitive harm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage of time alone is not sufficient to show undue prejudice. The court's factual findings (e.g., that the patent owner is an NPE and not directly competing) weigh against a finding of undue prejudice. The Board and courts examine whether prejudice is more than mere delay and whether the stay alleviates prejudice. Citations: Sec. First Innovations v. Google; Court Order findings regarding NPE status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence in Filing the Petition
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the petitioner filed the IPR with reasonable diligence given the litigation timeline and facts (considered under Factor 3 and in assessing petitions generally).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioner diligence supports institution where the petition was filed without undue delay and where the parallel litigation was in an early stage. Routine litigation actions by petitioner (e.g., filing a motion to dismiss) do not show lack of diligence sufficient to justify discretionary denial. Precedent: Stingray Group indicates timing of filing, when case was in early stage, does not weigh against institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and Weight of Trial Statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether median time-to-trial or other district-court statistics should be used to predict if a court trial will occur before the PTAB’s Final Written Decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trial statistics may be consulted but are not controlling. If a court has stayed its case and there is no scheduling order, statistical projections cannot be used to override clear evidence (e.g., a stay) that no trial will occur before the FWD. Relying solely on median trial projections when a stay exists is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel Under 35 U.S.C. § 315
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration that a petitioner will be estopped from raising any invalidity grounds that were raised or reasonably could have been raised in the IPR following a Final Written Decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The potential for estoppel reduces concerns about duplication of efforts and conflicting decisions and thus supports institution or reduces overlap concerns under Factor 4. This is a material consideration when district-court cases are stayed and when an IPR could simplify issues in litigation. Citation: ResMed Corp. discussion of estoppel.
